content: Based on body surface area (mg/m²), the actual daily dose in mice reached up to 5000 mg/kg/day when administered through food. In one strain of rats, dietary administration of doses exceeding the maximum tolerated dose for 22 months resulted in hyperplasia of the biliary tract, as well as cholangioma and adenocarcinoma of the intrahepatic biliary system. At lower doses, hyperplastic but not neoplastic lesions were observed. However, subsequent long-term dietary studies in a different strain of rats, using exposure levels equivalent to the maximum levels employed in the earlier experiment, did not demonstrate such hyperplastic or neoplastic changes in the liver. Mutagenesis: Tranexamic acid was neither mutagenic nor clastogenic in the in vitro Bacterial Reverse Mutation Assay (Ames test), the in vitro chromosome aberration test in Chinese hamster cells, or in in vivo chromosome aberration tests conducted in mice and rats. Impairment of Fertility: Reproductive studies in mice, rats, and rabbits showed no evidence of impaired fertility or adverse effects on the fetus due to tranexamic acid. In a rat embryo-fetal developmental toxicity study, tranexamic acid did not adversely affect embryo-fetal development when administered during the organogenesis period (gestation days 6 through 17) at doses equivalent to 1, 2, and 4 times the recommended human oral dose of 3900 mg/day. Similarly, in a perinatal-postnatal study in rats, tranexamic acid had no adverse effects on pup viability, growth, or development when administered from gestation day 6 through postnatal day 20 at the same dose multiples. These dose multiples were calculated based on body surface area (mg/m²), with actual daily doses in rats being 300, 750, or 1500 mg/kg/day. Animal Toxicology and/or Pharmacology Ocular Effects: In a 9-month toxicology study, dogs were administered tranexamic acid in food at doses of 0, 200, 600, or 1200 mg/kg/day, which correspond to approximately 2, 5, and 6 times the recommended human oral dose of 3900 mg/day based on AUC. At 6 times the human dose, some dogs developed reversible reddening and gelatinous discharge from the eyes. Ophthalmologic examination revealed reversible changes in the nictitating membrane/conjunctiva, and in some female dogs, inflammatory exudate was observed over the bulbar conjunctival mucosa. Histopathological examinations did not reveal any retinal alterations. No adverse effects were observed at 5 times the human dose. In other studies, focal areas of retinal degeneration were observed in cats, dogs, and rats following oral or intravenous tranexamic acid doses at 6-40 times the usual recommended human dose based on mg/m² (actual animal doses ranged from 250-1600 mg/kg/day). Clinical Studies: The efficacy and safety of tranexamic acid in treating heavy menstrual bleeding (HMB) were demonstrated in two randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled studies: one with a 3-cycle treatment duration and another with a 6-cycle treatment duration. HMB was defined as an average menstrual blood loss (MBL) of ≥80 mL, assessed using alkaline hematin analysis of collected sanitary products over two baseline menstrual cycles. Subjects were aged 18 to 49 years, with a mean age of approximately 40 years, had cyclic menses every 21-35 days, and a BMI of approximately 32 kg/m². On average, subjects had a history of HMB for about 10 years, and 40% had fibroids as determined by transvaginal ultrasound. Approximately 70% of subjects were Caucasian, 25% were Black, and 5% were Asian, Native American, Pacific Islander, or Other. Seven percent of all subjects were of Hispanic origin. In these studies, the primary outcome measure was menstrual blood loss (MBL), assessed using the alkaline hematin method. The endpoint was the change from baseline in MBL, calculated by subtracting the mean MBL during treatment from the mean pretreatment MBL. Key secondary outcome measures included limitations in social or leisure activities (LSLA), limitations in physical activities (LPA), and the occurrence of large stains (soiling beyond the undergarment). Three-Cycle Treatment Study: This study compared the effects of two doses of tranexamic acid (1950 mg and 3900 mg daily for up to 5 days during each menstrual period) versus placebo on MBL over a 3-cycle treatment duration. Of the 294 evaluable subjects, 115 received 1950 mg/day tranexamic acid, 112 received 3900 mg/day tranexamic acid, and 67 received placebo. All subjects took at least one dose of the study drug and had post-treatment data available. Results showed that MBL was statistically significantly reduced in patients treated with 3900 mg/day tranexamic acid compared to placebo. Study success also required achieving a reduction in MBL deemed clinically meaningful to the subjects. The 1950 mg/day dose did not meet the criteria for success. Tranexamic acid at 3900 mg/day also statistically significantly reduced limitations on social, leisure, and physical activities compared to placebo. However, no statistically significant treatment difference was observed in response rates for the number of large stains. Six-Cycle Treatment Study: This study compared the effects of tranexamic acid 3900 mg/day (administered daily for up to 5 days during each menstrual period) versus placebo on MBL over a 6-cycle treatment duration. Of the 187 evaluable subjects, 115 received tranexamic acid, and 72 received placebo. All subjects took at least one dose of the study drug and had post-treatment data available. Results demonstrated a statistically significant reduction in MBL in the tranexamic acid group compared to placebo.
